- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Q1 (Page 101):
    * [Q1] (conceptual): What is the difference between a reflex action and walking?
      Method: Reflex action is involuntary and controlled by spinal cord; walking is voluntary and controlled by cerebellum and cerebrum.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Receptor":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): Which of the following receptors is correctly matched with its function? (a) Gustatory - smell (b) Olfactory - taste (c) Gustatory - taste (d) Thermoreceptor - sight
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (c) Gustatory - taste
      -> Socratic Hint: Recall that tongue contains taste buds (gustatory receptors) and nose contains smell receptors (olfactory).
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): Define receptors. Where are they usually located?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Receptors are specialized tips of nerve cells that detect all information from our environment. They are usually located in our sense organs such as the inner ear, nose, tongue, skin, and eyes.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about how your body senses touch or heat.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Short Answer): Explain why olfactory and gustatory receptors are necessary for humans.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Olfactory receptors detect smell and gustatory receptors detect taste. These receptors allow us to perceive chemical stimuli in our environment, helping us identify food quality and avoid noxious substances.
      -> Socratic Hint: Relate this to Activity 6.1 regarding blocked nose and food taste.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Structured): Describe how information from the environment is detected and communicated in our body.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Information is detected by specialized receptors in sense organs. It is acquired at the dendritic tip of a nerve cell, setting off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. This travels from dendrite to cell body and along the axon.
      -> Socratic Hint: Trace the pathway from stimulus detection to electrical impulse generation.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): State the role of gustatory and olfactory receptors in human beings. (CBSE 2020)
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Gustatory receptors detect taste, while olfactory receptors detect smell.
      -> Socratic Hint: Keep definitions precise and direct.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Why does food taste bland when you have a severe cold? Explain based on receptors.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Taste heavily relies on smell. When suffering from a cold, mucus blocks olfactory receptors in the nose, preventing them from detecting volatile food odors, thereby diminishing the perceived taste.
      -> Socratic Hint: Connect smell and taste mechanisms discussed in Activity 6.1.
  * Concept #2 "Neuron":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): In a neuron, conversion of electrical signal to a chemical signal occurs at/in: (a) cell body (b) axonal end (c) dendritic tip (d) myelin sheath
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (b) axonal end
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about what is released at the end of the axon to cross the synapse.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): What is a synapse?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: A synapse is the narrow gap between the axon terminal of one neuron and the dendritic tip of the next neuron where chemical messengers bridge the gap.
      -> Socratic Hint: It acts as a junction between two neurons.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Short Answer): Trace the sequence of events during transmission of a nerve impulse across a synapse.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 1. Electrical impulse reaches axonal end. 2. Triggers release of neurotransmitter chemicals. 3. Chemicals cross synapse and start electrical impulse in next dendrite.
      -> Socratic Hint: Electrical -> Chemical -> Electrical.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Structured): Draw a neat diagram of a neuron and label: (i) Dendrite (ii) Cell body (iii) Axon (iv) Nerve ending. Explain the function of each.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Dendrite acquires information; cell body processes it; axon transmits impulse away; nerve ending releases chemicals.
      -> Socratic Hint: Draw clear branching dendrites, central soma, long axon, and terminal knobs.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): How is an electrical impulse generated and transmitted along a neuron? (CBSE 2019)
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Acquired at dendritic tip -> chemical reaction creates electrical impulse -> travels to cell body -> along axon to nerve ending.
      -> Socratic Hint: Outline the path from dendrite to axon.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Why are nerve impulses unidirectional across synapses?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Chemical substances (neurotransmitters) are released only from axon terminals and their receptors are present only on the post-synaptic dendritic membrane.
      -> Socratic Hint: Chemicals are only stored at axon ends.

key_concepts: Receptor: Specialized tips of nerve cells that detect information from the environment (e.g., gustatory for taste, olfactory for smell).
Neuron: Structural and functional unit of nervous tissue consisting of dendrites, cell body (cyton), and axon.
Synapse: The microscopic gap between two neurons where electrical impulses are converted into chemical signals.
Neuromuscular Junction: The site of transmission of electric impulse from motor neuron to muscle fiber.
success_criteria: Accurately trace the path of a nerve impulse from receptor to effector and explain the role of synapses.
subtopics: Synapse and Transmission of Nerve Impulse
chapter_notes: Nervous tissue is composed of an organized network of neurons specialized for conducting information via electrical impulses. All information from the environment is detected by receptors in sense organs. The dendritic tip acquires information, creating an electrical impulse traveling through the cell body and axon. At axon terminals, chemicals cross the synapse to propagate the impulse to the next neuron or muscle/gland cell.

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:

    * [Q5] (conceptual): What is the role of the brain in reflex action?
      Method: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord itself for quick responses, though information also reaches the brain for record/awareness.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Reflex Action":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): Which of the following is a reflex action? (a) Writing (b) Typing (c) Knee-jerk response (d) Riding a bicycle
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (c) Knee-jerk response
      -> Socratic Hint: Reflex actions are sudden, involuntary responses without conscious thought.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): What is a reflex arc?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: The pathway of communication from a sensory neuron through the spinal cord to a motor neuron in a reflex action is called a reflex arc.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think of the shortest path from stimulus to response.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Short Answer): Why have reflex arcs evolved in animals?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Thinking process in the brain is not instantaneous. Reflex arcs provide quick, efficient responses to dangerous stimuli (like heat) where immediate survival is paramount, bypassing complex brain processing.
      -> Socratic Hint: Speed is key for survival.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Structured): Trace the sequence of events (reflex arc) when a person touches a hot object.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 1. Receptors in skin detect heat (stimulus). 2. Sensory neuron carries signal to spinal cord. 3. Relay neuron processes in spinal cord. 4. Motor neuron carries signal to effector (muscle in arm). 5. Muscle pulls hand away.
      -> Socratic Hint: Receptor -> Sensory -> Spinal Cord -> Motor -> Effector.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): Define reflex action. Give an example. (CBSE 2020)
      -> Ideal Model Answer: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. Example: Pulling hand back from a hot flame.
      -> Socratic Hint: Keep it direct and standard.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Even after complex brains evolved, reflex arcs continue to exist. Give reasons.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Brain thinking is complex and takes time. Reflex arcs operate instantaneously at the spinal cord level, offering vital protection against sudden hazards before conscious thought can occur.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about split-second survival needs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a reflex action? (a) Writing (b) Typing (c) Knee-jerk response (d) Riding a bicycle
questions.ideal_answer: (c) Knee-jerk response
questions.socratic_hint: Reflex actions are sudden, involuntary responses without conscious thought.

questions.question: What is a reflex arc?
questions.ideal_answer: The pathway of communication from a sensory neuron through the spinal cord to a motor neuron in a reflex action is called a reflex arc.
questions.socratic_hint: Think of the shortest path from stimulus to response.

questions.question: Why have reflex arcs evolved in animals?
questions.ideal_answer: Thinking process in the brain is not instantaneous. Reflex arcs provide quick, efficient responses to dangerous stimuli (like heat) where immediate survival is paramount, bypassing complex brain processing.
questions.socratic_hint: Speed is key for survival.

questions.question: Trace the sequence of events (reflex arc) when a person touches a hot object.
questions.ideal_answer: 1. Receptors in skin detect heat (stimulus). 2. Sensory neuron carries signal to spinal cord. 3. Relay neuron processes in spinal cord. 4. Motor neuron carries signal to effector (muscle in arm). 5. Muscle pulls hand away.
questions.socratic_hint: Receptor -> Sensory -> Spinal Cord -> Motor -> Effector.

questions.question: Define reflex action. Give an example. (CBSE 2020)
questions.ideal_answer: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. Example: Pulling hand back from a hot flame.
questions.socratic_hint: Keep it direct and standard.

questions.question: Even after complex brains evolved, reflex arcs continue to exist. Give reasons.
questions.ideal_answer: Brain thinking is complex and takes time. Reflex arcs operate instantaneously at the spinal cord level, offering vital protection against sudden hazards before conscious thought can occur.
questions.socratic_hint: Think about split-second survival needs.

questions.solution_method: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord itself for quick responses, though information also reaches the brain for record/awareness.

Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Comprises cranial nerves (from brain) and spinal nerves (from spinal cord).
Fore-brain: Main thinking part of the brain; contains regions for hearing, smell, sight, and association.
Cerebellum: Part of the hind-brain responsible for precision of voluntary actions and body posture/balance.
Medulla: Part of the hind-brain controlling involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting.

description: Examine immediate responses, tropic movements (phototropism, geotropism), and plant growth regulators (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid).
ai_system_prompt_context:

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:

    * [Q1] (conceptual): What are plant hormones?
      Method: Chemical compounds synthesized by plants to help coordinate growth, development, and responses to the environment.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Tropism":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): The bending of shoot towards light is known as: (a) Geotropism (b) Phototropism (c) Hydrotropism (d) Chemotropism
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (b) Phototropism
      -> Socratic Hint: Photo refers to light.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): Define geotropism with an example.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Geotropism is the directional growth of plant parts in response to gravity. Example: Plant roots grow downwards into the soil (positive geotropism).
      -> Socratic Hint: Geo relates to gravity/earth.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Short Answer): Explain how plant roots show positive geotropism and shoots show negative geotropism.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Roots grow downward in response to gravity's pull (positive geotropism), whereas shoots grow upward against gravity (negative geotropism).
      -> Socratic Hint: Compare directions of root and shoot growth relative to earth.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Structured): How does phototropism occur in plants? Explain with reference to auxin.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: When light falls from one side, auxin diffuses towards the shady side of the shoot. Higher auxin concentration on the shady side stimulates cells to grow longer there, causing the shoot to bend towards the light source.
      -> Socratic Hint: Auxin accumulates away from light and accelerates cell elongation on the dark side.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): Name the plant hormone responsible for cell elongation and phototropic bending. (CBSE 2019)
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Auxin
      -> Socratic Hint: Synthesized at the shoot tip.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Why do tendrils coil around a support when they touch it?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: When tendrils touch a support, the part in contact does not grow as rapidly as the part away from the support, causing the tendril to circle and cling around the object.
      -> Socratic Hint: Differential growth rate on contact.

key_concepts: Tropism: Directional growth movement of plants in response to environmental stimuli (light, gravity, water).
Phototropism: Directional growth movement in response to light (shoots bend towards light, positive phototropism).
Geotropism: Growth movement in response to gravity (roots grow down, positive geotropism).
Auxin: Plant hormone synthesized at shoot tips that promotes cell elongation and mediates phototropism.
success_criteria: Describe the mechanism of phototropism and list the functions of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, and abscisic acid.
chapter_notes: Plants lack nervous and muscular systems, relying on chemical communication and turgor changes. Sensitive plants (Mimosa pudica) show immediate responses via water loss/gain in cells. Growth-dependent movements include tropisms: phototropism (light response via auxin redistribution), geotropism (gravity response), and chemotropism (chemical response like pollen tube growth). Plant hormones: Auxin (cell elongation), Gibberellins (stem growth), Cytokinins (cell division), Abscisic Acid (growth inhibition/wilting).

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 6.1 & 6.2, p. 6 & p. 9): (a) What is the difference between a reflex action and walking? (b) What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
worked_examples.given: Somatic voluntary locomotion vs involuntary spinal reflex arcs; Neurotransmitter synaptic transmission.
worked_examples.formula: Reflex Arc: Receptor -> Sensory Neuron -> Spinal Relay Neuron -> Motor Neuron -> Effector. Synaptic transmission: Chemical neurotransmitters (acetylcholine) diffuse across synaptic cleft.
worked_examples.substitution: Involuntary spinal arc vs cerebral cortical motor planning.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Reflex Action vs Walking:
1. Reflex action: Rapid, involuntary, automatic motor response to an immediate external hazard (e.g. withdrawing hand from hot flame). Coordinated primarily by the SPINAL CORD without prior conscious brain intervention.
2. Walking: Voluntary, intentional, learned locomotor action coordinated and controlled consciously by the FOREBRAIN (cerebral motor cortex and cerebellum for balance).
(b) Events at the Synapse:
When an electrical nerve impulse reaches the axon terminal of the pre-synaptic neuron, it triggers synaptic vesicles to release chemical neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) into the microscopic gap (synaptic cleft). The neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft and bind to specific receptor sites on the dendrite membrane of the post-synaptic neuron, initiating a new electrical impulse. This chemical bridge ensures strictly UNIDIRECTIONAL signal transmission.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Reflex action is an automatic involuntary spinal response; walking is a conscious voluntary action controlled by the forebrain; (b) Electrical impulse releases chemical neurotransmitters across the synaptic cleft to initiate a new impulse in the next neuron.

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question & Exercise (Section 6.3 & p. 13): (a) What are plant hormones (phytohormones)? Give examples of growth promoters and growth inhibitors. (b) How does phototropism occur in plant shoots?
worked_examples.given: Plant hormonal signaling; Shoot phototropism mechanism.
worked_examples.formula: Auxin differential elongation on shaded side: Stem bends toward light ($L_{\text{shaded}} > L_{\text{illuminated}}$).
worked_examples.substitution: Auxin redistribution away from unilateral light source.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Plant hormones are chemical coordination substances synthesized in minute quantities at shoot/root tips that regulate cell division, elongation, and differentiation.
- Growth Promoters: Auxins (cell elongation, apical dominance), Gibberellins (stem elongation, seed germination), Cytokinins (active cell division, stomatal opening).
- Growth Inhibitor: Abscisic Acid / ABA (induces dormancy, leaf wilting/fall, stomatal closure under drought stress).
(b) Mechanism of Phototropism: When unilateral sunlight shines on one side of a plant shoot, auxin synthesized at the shoot tip diffuses toward the SHADED SIDE of the stem. The higher concentration of auxin stimulates the cells on the shaded side to grow and elongate faster than cells on the illuminated side. This asymmetric elongation causes the shoot stem to curve and bend toward the light source (positive phototropism).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Promoters: Auxin, Gibberellin, Cytokinin; Inhibitor: Abscisic acid (ABA); (b) Auxin migrates to the shaded side, stimulating faster elongation and causing the shoot to bend towards light.

questions.question: Which of the following is a plant hormone? (a) Insulin (b) Thyroxin (c) Oestrogen (d) Cytokinin
questions.ideal_answer: (d) Cytokinin
questions.socratic_hint: Check plant vs animal hormone lists.

questions.question: The gap between two neurons is called a: (a) dendrite (b) synapse (c) axon (d) impulse
questions.ideal_answer: (b) synapse
questions.socratic_hint: Junction between neurons.

questions.question: Compare and contrast nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals.
questions.ideal_answer: Nervous: Uses electrical impulses via neurons; very fast; reaches specific connected cells; short-lived. Hormonal: Uses chemical messengers via blood; slower; reaches all body cells; long-lasting effects.
questions.socratic_hint: Compare speed, medium, and target specificity.

questions.question: What is the difference between the manner in which movement takes place in a sensitive plant and the movement in our legs?
questions.ideal_answer: Sensitive plant movement is independent of growth, caused by turgor pressure changes (water movement in/out of cells) in response to touch, occurring very rapidly. Movement in our legs is voluntary, controlled by the CNS, involving muscular tissue where specialized proteins change shape in response to nerve impulses.
questions.socratic_hint: Compare turgor/water-based vs muscle/protein-based movement.

questions.question: How do auxins promote the growth of a tendril around a support? (CBSE 2020)
questions.ideal_answer: When tendrils touch a support, auxin redistributes, causing cells away from the support to grow faster than cells in contact, resulting in coiling around the support.
questions.socratic_hint: Differential growth rate on touch.

questions.question: Why is a system of control and coordination essential in multicellular organisms?
questions.ideal_answer: Multicellular organisms have specialized tissues and organs that must work together in an integrated, synchronized manner to respond appropriately to external environmental changes and maintain internal homeostasis.
questions.socratic_hint: Think about division of labor in complex bodies.
